THE WORLD / 03 / THE PLACES INNOCENCE LOST

One house.
An entire world.

To the family, it is an ordinary home. To the toys, every familiar threshold is a journey worth taking.

THE GEOGRAPHY OF MEMORYPREPRODUCTION / 2026
CHAPTER 03 — THE HOUSEHOLDTOY-SCALE WORLD DESIGNPHYSICAL FLOOR PLAN NOT YET LOCKED

THE WORLD DESIGN PRINCIPLE KEEP IT HUMAN

Not fantasy rooms.
Real places, re-seen.

The house should remain coherent and recognizable. The toy-size camera turns everyday objects into monumental geography without changing what those objects really are.

01

Recognizable geography

Rooms must connect through a verified floor plan. Story progression does not prove where doors, halls, or gates are located.

02

Physical toy identity

Kip’s wheels, Rallo’s limited flight, Jayze’s humanoid reach, and Jonnie’s heavy exoskeleton must all fit the same world.

03

One home, two meanings

Outward and return scenes should preserve familiar objects while changing the characters’ purposes, decisions, and framing.

THE ROUTE STORY ORDER — NOT ARCHITECTURAL SURVEY

CJ’S TOYS→HALLWAY→KITCHEN→OUTSIDE→ALLEY↩HOME

The plot establishes a sequence of major locations. Exact adjacencies, intervening rooms, and outdoor access still require a physical layout pass.

01
LOCATION 01 / HOME BEFORE THE CRISIS

CJ’S TOY AREA

The familiar world

The opening establishes toy community, warmth, playful combat, and the objects that make CJ’s room recognizably his. Floorboards, carpet, shelves, and furniture should be navigable landmarks rather than generic props.

ON THE RETURNReturn scenes can echo familiar sightlines while showing a more considerate and capable party.

DESIGN OPPORTUNITYOpening navigation, early battles, toy-scale visual grammar.

02
LOCATION 02 / DISTANCE BECOMES DANGER

THE LONG HALLWAY

First limit of confidence

A predominantly straight domestic corridor whose length, doorframes, and repeating baseboards turn distance into exposure. The rescue near the far end is associated with CJ’s father’s belongings.

ON THE RETURNThe same hallway can become a space for planning and attention to vulnerable companions.

DESIGN OPPORTUNITYLong-distance framing, formation, grounded rescue staging.

03
LOCATION 03 / CARE UNDER PRESSURE

THE KITCHEN

The second intervention

Household appliances, cabinets, furniture legs, and the way outside form a physically legible environment. Belongings associated with CJ’s mother intervene when the threat intensifies.

ON THE RETURNPreviously incidental signs of daily care take on greater meaning as the toys become protectors.

DESIGN OPPORTUNITYEnvironmental obstacles, directional combat, near-exit encounter.

04
LOCATION 04 / THE BOUNDARY OF HOME

PORCH & THRESHOLD

A crossing between worlds

Door sills, steps, railings, and porch surfaces are enormous topographical features at toy size. The exact architecture is not yet validated. Crossing outside should feel like leaving a form of shelter.

ON THE RETURNThe threshold becomes a deliberate passage back toward the family.

DESIGN OPPORTUNITYTraversal for wheels, armor, flight, and humanoid movement.

05
LOCATION 05 / BEYOND THE WALLS

THE BACKYARD

Exposed and uncertain

Grass blades, soil, roots, cracks, and outdoor objects make a familiar yard difficult terrain. The house should remain visually recognizable when the physical sightlines allow it.

ON THE RETURNOn the return, the same obstacles become routes the team can understand and solve together.

DESIGN OPPORTUNITYMixed-terrain navigation, formations, scale comparisons.

06
LOCATION 06 / THE FARTHEST POINT

THE ALLEY

A choice with no certainty

An ordinary alley, not automatically a visually evil path. Grandparents’ heirlooms rescue the group. The toys can see the road stretching onward and the direction back toward their family.

ON THE RETURNThe journey reverses here. No elder commands the toys to choose; the decision to return is their own.

DESIGN OPPORTUNITYA quiet turning point, earned agency, clear views in both directions.

07
LOCATION 07 / KNOWN THROUGH NEW EYES

THE HOME AGAIN

Protect, do not merely survive

Returning through established spaces creates purposeful variation rather than unrelated new levels. The toys recognize where help once arrived—and what they can now offer in return.

ON THE RETURNTheir changed behavior, not simply brighter lighting, expresses maturity.

DESIGN OPPORTUNITYMirrored encounters, party coordination, reciprocal protection.

DESIGN LOGIC ONE ENVIRONMENT, FOUR BODIES

The house has
its own rules.

A floor gap, shelf edge, kitchen threshold, or patch of grass cannot mean the same thing to every toy. Traversal is part of character identity. Solutions must come from believable geometry, the toys’ abilities, or cooperation—not unmotivated teleportation.

JAYZEAction-figure reach, weapon clearance, conventional foot movement.
KIPWheel contact, traction, ramp angle, ground clearance.
RALLOLow-altitude flight, ceiling clearance, positional utility.
JONNIEExoskeleton width, mass, turning radius, protective positioning.
RELATIVE SCALE / STILL SUBJECT TO APPROVAL
